title: Revelation and Prophetic Cognition in the Philosophy of Avicenna
content: Revelation occupies a significant position at the intersection of metaphysics, psychology, and political philosophy in Avicenna’s account of prophecy. Building upon questions developed by al-Fārābī, Avicenna explains prophetic knowledge through the exceptional perfection of human cognitive faculties and their relationship with the intelligible order. Although God remains the ultimate source of revelation, its reception is understood within a hierarchy of intellectual and celestial mediation. Prophecy thus represents a distinctive realization of human capacities rather than a phenomenon wholly external to human nature. This article examines the relationship between emanation, the rational soul, intellectual perfection, and the imaginative reception of revealed knowledge. Particular attention is given to the distinction between intellectual apprehension and the representation of intelligible content through images, whether during sleep or in waking experience. The discussion also considers the practical significance of prophecy: the prophet communicates knowledge in forms capable of guiding collective life and shaping moral and political conduct. Avicenna’s account consequently presents revelation as both an exceptional mode of cognition and a foundation for the public responsibilities of prophetic leadership. At the same time, the possibility of related experiences among spiritually disciplined individuals requires a distinction between extraordinary cognition and the full capacities associated with the prophetic mission.
